title: Island Perimeter
description: Brute force to optimized: checking all four neighbor directions versus checking only top and left to avoid double-counting.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a grid where 1 represents land and 0 represents water, forming exactly one island (a connected group of land cells, with no lakes, no diagonal connections), return the perimeter of that island.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","grid of 0s and 1s, exactly one island"],["Output","The perimeter of the island"],["Key Insight","Every land cell contributes 4 sides by default; every shared edge between two adjacent land cells removes 2 from the total (1 from each cell's count)"],["Constraints","Up to 100 by 100 grid"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Perimeter of a shape on a grid\"","Counting exposed edges: every land cell contributes 4 sides, minus 2 for every pair of directly adjacent land cells (their shared internal edge)"]]}

blocks.text: Think of each land cell as independently contributing 4 unit sides to the total perimeter. Whenever two land cells are directly adjacent (sharing an edge), that shared edge is INTERNAL to the island, not part of the perimeter, so it must be subtracted. Since each shared edge is counted twice if checking all 4 neighbors of every cell (once from each side), checking only 2 directions per cell (say, top and left) and subtracting 2 per match avoids double-counting entirely.

blocks.title: Analogy: Measuring the Outer Fence Needed Around a Cluster of Adjacent Plots
blocks.text: Picture measuring how much outer fencing is needed around a cluster of adjacent land plots. Each individual plot would need fencing on all 4 sides alone, but wherever two plots sit directly next to each other, the fence between them is unnecessary (both plots already border each other), so that shared side is removed from the total needed.

blocks.caption: Every land cell contributes 4 sides; subtract 2 for every direct land-land neighbor pair

blocks.text: Result: 4 (a single land cell contributes all 4 of its sides).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Start a running perimeter total at 0.

Observation 2: For every land cell encountered, add 4 (its default contribution as an isolated square).

Observation 3: Check ONLY the cell directly ABOVE and the cell directly to the LEFT (not all 4 directions, to avoid double-counting the SAME shared edge from both sides); if either neighbor is also land, subtract 2 from the total (removing that shared internal edge's contribution from BOTH cells involved).

Observation 4: After processing every cell in the grid this way, the running total is exactly the island's perimeter.
This leads to a single scan over the grid, adding 4 per land cell and subtracting 2 per direct land-land neighbor found (checking only top and left).
For each land cell, check all FOUR neighboring directions individually, adding 1 to the perimeter for each neighbor that is water or out of bounds.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking all four directions per cell directly counts every exposed edge.

This checks each internal shared edge from BOTH sides (redundant but still correct); checking only top and left per cell, subtracting 2 per match, achieves the same result with half the neighbor checks.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols), checking 4 neighbors per land cell.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: checking only 2 directions per cell (top and left), and subtracting 2 for each land-land match, achieves the identical result with fewer checks per cell.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Initialize perimeter to 0. For each cell in the grid: if it is land, add 4 to the perimeter. Then check the cell directly ABOVE; if it exists and is also land, subtract 2 (removing that shared edge's double-counted contribution). Similarly check the cell directly to the LEFT; if it exists and is also land, subtract 2. After scanning the entire grid this way, the running total is the final perimeter.
Scan the grid once, adding 4 per land cell and subtracting 2 per direct land-land neighbor found, checking only top and left.

blocks.text: Every land cell independently contributing 4 sides correctly counts the perimeter of a completely isolated single cell; checking only the top and left neighbors (never right or bottom) and subtracting 2 for each land-land match correctly removes exactly ONE shared internal edge's double contribution per adjacent pair, without ever needing to check the same pair of cells from both directions.

blocks.text: Island Perimeter is a clean introduction to the "count exposed edges by subtracting shared edges" technique on a grid, foundational for more advanced grid connectivity problems.

items: Checking all 4 directions AND subtracting for every match, which double-subtracts each shared edge instead of just once.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "perimeter of a connected shape on a grid", think: every cell contributes 4 sides, minus 2 per shared internal edge.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(rows times cols); checking only top and left per cell is a slightly more elegant way to avoid double-counting shared edges.

items: Pattern: counting exposed edges on a grid by subtracting shared internal edges.
Core Idea: every land cell contributes 4 sides; subtract 2 for every direct land-land neighbor pair found (checking only top and left avoids double-counting).
Time: O(rows times cols) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: checking only 2 directions per cell (not 4) avoids double-subtracting the same shared edge.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy grid-counting problem.
One line memory trick: 4 per land cell, minus 2 per shared edge.
